enrichment.short_title: Refugee Legal Centre: interim protective costs order for Harmondsworth fast-track challenge
key_facts: The Refugee Legal Centre challenged the lawfulness of the Harmondsworth fast-track pilot for straightforward single male asylum claims, where interviews and refusals occur within days.
Collins J had held the present system was not unlawful despite concerns about tight timescales for legal preparation.
The Centre sought a protective costs order before a full Court of Appeal hearing on the criteria for such orders under the CPR.
Counsel acted pro bono and the Centre would not seek costs if successful; the Home Office resisted any protective order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application before Brooke LJ for a protective costs order ahead of a listed full-court hearing on protective costs criteria and the substantive appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Protective costs order granted for the imminent application hearing only, on the understanding the Centre would not seek costs against the Secretary of State if successful on that application.
enrichment.ratio: Where public-interest litigation is brought pro bono by a not-for-profit body representing vulnerable asylum seekers against the state, it may be appropriate to make an interim protective costs order pending full argument on the proper CPR approach to protective costs orders.
legal_issues: Whether a protective costs order should protect the Refugee Legal Centre for the upcoming costs-criteria hearing
Whether systemic challenges to asylum fast-track procedures should be brought by individual legal aid cases instead
Application of pre-CPR and post-CPR authorities on pre-emptive or protective costs orders

enrichment.short_title: South Cambridgeshire v persons unknown: section 187B planning injunction at Smithy Fen
key_facts: South Cambridgeshire District Council sought injunctions restraining deposit of hardcore, stationing of caravans and non-agricultural use on Plots 1-11 Victoria View, Smithy Fen, Cottenham.
The county court judge dismissed the application, doubting power to grant relief against persons unknown despite serious local gypsy/traveller encroachment problems.
Enforcement notices from 1999 had been upheld on appeal but unauthorised activity continued between authorised caravan areas.
The council proposed service by documents in plastic envelopes nailed to stakes on each plot.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from Cambridge County Court against refusal of a section 187B injunction against persons unknown.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the court held it had power to grant the injunction once the claim form identified defendants by conduct rather than subjective intention, subject to final drafting of service provisions.
enrichment.ratio: Section 187B and County Court Rule Order 49 permit planning injunctions against persons unknown where the claim form describes them with sufficient particularity by reference to conduct on identified land; subjective 'proposing' language should be replaced with 'causing or permitting'.
legal_issues: Whether the county court had jurisdiction to grant a section 187B injunction against persons unknown
Proper identification and service of defendants unknown under CPR Part 6 and Order 49
Whether expediency/necessity was established on the Smithy Fen evidence

enrichment.short_title: Dumford v Atlantrybflot: security for costs on Russian guarantor appeal
key_facts: Dumford obtained summary judgment for about £1.9 million plus interest against OAO Atlantrybflot on fishing-vessel loan guarantees.
OAO contended the true guarantor was subsidiary ZAO Atlantrybflot, not OAO, because guarantees were signed for ZAO but gave OAO's Kaliningrad address.
After judgment OAO sold eleven fishing vessels to associated company Finval; Dumford alleged asset dissipation to frustrate enforcement in Russia.
OceanProduct had funded OAO's litigation through Baker & McKenzie without reimbursement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications on appeal for stay of execution, security for costs, and CPR 52.9 conditions requiring payment of the judgment debt into court.
enrichment.outcome: Conditions requiring payment of the judgment sum refused; security for costs of £38,000 ordered by 22 October 2004 with appeal dismissed if not paid; stay refused subject to Dumford undertaking to pay recovered sums into court; all application costs ordered costs in the appeal.
enrichment.ratio: CPR 52.9 conditions requiring payment of the whole judgment debt into court as a condition of proceeding are rare; absent compelling evidence of asset dissipation, foreign residence alone and group-company funding do not justify such draconian conditions, though full security for appeal costs reflecting Russian enforcement difficulty may be ordered.
legal_issues: Whether OAO should pay the judgment debt into court under CPR 52.9 as a condition of appealing
Whether vessel sales to Finval were asset dissipation or ordinary business restructuring
Quantum and timing of security for costs for a Russian appellant
Whether execution should be stayed pending appeal

enrichment.short_title: W Healthcare NHS Trust v KH: PEG reinsertion and best interests of MS patient
key_facts: KH, aged 59 with advanced multiple sclerosis, had relied on a PEG feeding tube for five years until it dislodged accidentally in August 2004.
She lacked capacity and could not swallow safely; clinicians unanimously supported reinsertion but her family unanimously opposed it.
Family and friends gave evidence she had repeatedly said she did not want to be kept alive by machines or when she no longer recognised relatives.
Coleridge J had granted the Trust's application; he gave leave to appeal describing the decision as borderline.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent same-day appeal from a High Court declaration permitting reinsertion of a PEG tube for artificial nutrition.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; reinsertion held lawful as there was no sufficiently clear advance directive and death by withdrawal of nutrition would not be in KH's best interests.
enrichment.ratio: Where an incapacitated patient has expressed general wishes against machine prolongation of life, those statements do not amount to a clear advance refusal of PEG feeding unless they specifically address withdrawal of nutrition and the nature of death by starvation; absent such a directive the best-interests test applies and intolerability is the touchstone, with doubt resolved in favour of preserving life.
legal_issues: Whether KH's earlier statements constituted a binding advance directive refusing PEG reinsertion
Whether withdrawal of PEG feeding was in her best interests
Distinction between best-interests and substituted-judgment approaches after Re F
Application of HE v A Hospital NHS Trust and Burke v GMC guidance
linked_authorities: Re T (Adult: Refusal of Treatment) [1993] Fam 95
HE v A Hospital NHS Trust [2003] 2 FLR 408

enrichment.short_title: Jeyapragash v IAT: consent remittal and Court of Appeal listing practice
key_facts: The appellant challenged an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision on whether explicit findings were required as to torture suffered in Sri Lanka before assessing return risk.
On the eve of hearing the parties agreed the IAT decision should be quashed and the appeal remitted to a differently constituted tribunal.
Brooke LJ criticised late Home Office settlements that prevented effective pre-reading and relisting under the new July 2004 Practice Direction.
The court required attendance to explain non-compliance rather than granting consent orders administratively.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Listed Court of Appeal hearing at which parties sought a consent order quashing the IAT decision and remitting the appeal.
enrichment.outcome: By consent the IAT decision was quashed, the appeal remitted to a fresh tribunal, and no order for costs save assessment under Legal Services Costs Regulations.
enrichment.ratio: Under the July 2004 Court of Appeal Practice Direction parties must settle or clarify their position at least seven days before hearing so judges can pre-read; the court will refuse administrative consent orders where the Practice Direction is breached and may require attendance and apply costs consequences.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT erred in failing to make explicit findings on torture
Compliance with the new Court of Appeal Practice Direction on skeleton arguments and bundles
Appropriate response to late consent settlements by the Home Office

enrichment.short_title: X v Caerphilly: SEN tribunal appeal on therapy provision for learning-disabled pupil
key_facts: Y, a 15-year-old with severe learning and language difficulties, had a statement proposing placement at a mainstream school's attached specialist centre.
His parents appealed, seeking residential specialist schooling with direct speech and language therapy and occupational therapy.
Conflicting professional evidence addressed whether direct weekly SLT sessions were an educational need and whether OT should appear in Part 3 rather than Part 5 of the statement.
After a breakdown at a Welsh-medium mainstream school, the Centre placement showed marked behavioural improvement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal on a point of law from a Special Educational Needs and Disability Tribunal decision dismissing the parents' appeal against Y's statement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; tribunal decision set aside and appeal remitted to a differently constituted tribunal; LEA ordered to pay costs.
enrichment.ratio: Direct speech and language therapy for a child whose language difficulties align with general learning disability is normally educational provision under the SEN Code of Practice unless exceptional reasons exist; a tribunal must give reasoned justification for rejecting expert recommendations, and occupational therapy addressing Part 2 learning skills belongs in Part 3 not Part 5.
legal_issues: Whether Y required direct speech and language therapy as an educational need
Whether the tribunal adequately reasoned its rejection of Arnaud's and Male's SLT recommendations
Whether occupational therapy for social interaction and independence skills was educational provision
Adequacy of the statement and tribunal reasons

enrichment.short_title: Hamsher v SoS: natural justice at Triyoga weekend-hours planning hearing

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Hearings Procedure) (England) Rules 2000

key_facts: Triyoga appealed successfully to extend weekend yoga class hours at 6 Erskine Road, NW3, subject to window and blind conditions for neighbour amenity.
Claimant Mr Hamsher, whose garden abutted the site, challenged the Inspector's decision under section 288.
He had not seen Triyoga's acoustic report before the hearing and complained of inadequate natural justice.
Camden notified him of the appeal but did not expressly inform him of his Rule 6(6) right to inspect hearing documents.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 application to quash an Inspector's decision allowing variation of planning conditions after a planning hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed on all grounds; claimant not a statutory party, hearing fair without adjournment, and enforceability views of a council officer not a material consideration requiring specific mention.
enrichment.ratio: An adjoining objector who responds to site notices is not a 'statutory party' entitled to service of hearing statements under Rule 2 limb (2); fairness at a planning hearing does not require the Inspector to offer an adjournment where the objector participated in discussion without requesting time to read documents or commission rival expert evidence.
legal_issues: Whether the claimant was a statutory party under the Hearings Procedure Rules
Whether failure to serve or disclose the acoustic report breached natural justice
Whether the Inspector should have offered an adjournment under Dyason principles
Whether the Inspector ignored a material consideration on enforceability of conditions
linked_authorities: Dyason v Secretary of State for the Environment [1998] 2 PLR 54

enrichment.short_title: George Wimpey v SoS: Morpeth housing shortfall and previously developed land
key_facts: George Wimpey appealed against non-determination of a scheme for 187 dwellings on land south of County Hall, Morpeth.
The Inspector recommended grant, finding a housing shortfall exceeding 200 dwellings and that Areas 2-3 were previously developed land within County Hall's curtilage.
The Secretary of State refused permission, treating Areas 2-3 as greenfield and dismissing housing need as insignificant.
The local plan acknowledged longer-term potential for the site but did not allocate Areas 2-3.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to the Secretary of State's decision refusing planning permission contrary to the Inspector's recommendation after public inquiry.
enrichment.outcome: Decision quashed on housing-land availability grounds; Secretary of State had failed to address the Inspector's shortfall findings and their interaction with other reasons; previously developed land and open-space grounds rejected.
enrichment.ratio: A decision letter must expressly grapple with an Inspector's central findings on housing shortfall where they drive the planning balance; referring only to a minor updated council shortfall figure while ignoring inquiry conclusions on a 200-plus dwelling deficit is a fatal flaw, and housing need is not independent of whether land is previously developed.
legal_issues: Whether the Secretary of State ignored the Inspector's housing shortfall conclusions
Whether Areas 2 and 3 were previously developed land within County Hall's curtilage under PPG3 Annex C
Whether Rule 17(5) inquiry procedure required consultation on curtilage disagreement
Weight given to loss of informal open space and sports provision
linked_authorities: Attorney General ex rel Sutcliffe v Calderdale Borough Council [1983] 46 P&CR 399

enrichment.short_title: Cottle v SoS: section 288 challenge to loft extension design refusal
key_facts: Mr Cottle appealed against Bath and North East Somerset Council's refusal of a dormer extension providing shower and toilet facilities to an existing loft conversion.
The Inspector dismissed the appeal, finding the scheme was not good design.
The claimant complained of inconsistent treatment because similar dormer extensions had been permitted on neighbouring houses.
He appeared in person and accepted the limited scope of section 288 review after explanation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 application to quash an Inspector's decision dismissing a householder planning appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; inconsistent council decisions on other properties could not show the Inspector acted unfairly or unlawfully, and no bias was alleged or evidenced against the decision-maker.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 288 the High Court may intervene only for error of law or procedural non-compliance causing substantial prejudice; perceived inconsistency in how a local planning authority treats other applications is not evidence that an Inspector determining a particular appeal acted unfairly or with bias.
legal_issues: Whether the Inspector's design conclusion involved unfairness or natural justice breach
Whether comparator approvals elsewhere showed bias or error of law
Scope of section 288 review of planning Inspector decisions
